c-mh-v4-loop-retrain-suppress.quote: The 2011 patent operated by attaching a bit to each Fetch Prediction entry, essentially marking whether the entry changes frequently; the 2017 patent operates by detecting if the branch to be retrained is within a tight loop.

c-mh-v4-tage-5-cycles.text: As of the 2017 loop-retrain patent, the TAGE direction predictor takes up to five cycles to give a prediction
c-mh-v4-tage-5-cycles.quote: the predictions of the loop might change within the maximum of (at the time of the patent) five cycles it might take TAGE

c-mh-v4-a6-fetch-32b.text: Per the 2012 fetch-width-predictor patent, Apple's maximum fetch width around the A6 was 32 bytes
c-mh-v4-a6-fetch-32b.quote: Even as of 2012 (so around A6), Apple's maximum Fetch Width appears to have been 32 bytes.
c-mh-v4-a6-fetch-32b.notes: US20140075156A1. Handley gives 8 instructions, or 16 Thumb instructions in that ARMv7 core.

c-mh-v4-nfp-index-tag.text: Per the 2012 patent, the fetch-predictor index XORs a few higher PC bits into the low bits, and each entry is tagged with higher PC bits so aliased entries are caught
c-mh-v4-nfp-index-tag.quote: The index into the Fetch table appears to have a few higher order bits xor'd in with the low bits ... Each entry in the Fetch Predictor is tagged by higher order bits of the PC.

c-mh-v4-nfp-overflow-groups.text: Fetch groups longer than the maximum are split: an extra predictor entry keyed at the cut point covers the rest (e.g. a 30-instruction body becomes 16 + 14)
c-mh-v4-nfp-overflow-groups.quote: for the address that corresponds to 16 instructions into the long Fetch Group, create a fake entry that corresponds to the next 14 instructions. ... Apple appears to be following this traditional answer.

c-mh-v4-nfp-longer-trace.text: Around a short, predictable forward branch the fetch predictor keeps the longer (not-taken) trace; when the branch is taken the extra instructions are deleted from the instruction queue, without a resteer
c-mh-v4-nfp-longer-trace.quote: The Fetch predictor, in this case, is retrained to the longer trace, but not retrained to the shorter trace, so it will always pull in the longer trace.

c-mh-v4-sof-fallback.text: The scan-on-fill predictor is consulted when the next fetch target misses the main fetch predictor: an unconditional exit gives the whole trace, a return uses the RAS, a conditional exit uses static heuristics
c-mh-v4-sof-fallback.quote: suppose I don’t find it; then I look in the Scan-on-Fill predictor and hopefully I can use some of the information there to construct the next trace.
c-mh-v4-sof-fallback.notes: US10747539B1 (2016); Handley likens it to Boomerang (2017).

c-mh-v4-sof-scan-timing.text: Scan-on-fill results live in a predictor in the fetch unit, filled on free L1I cycles between a line's prefetch and its first use, so a line used too soon may not yet be scanned
c-mh-v4-sof-scan-timing.quote: So the Scan-on-Fill processing does not happen when a line enters the L1I, it happens (hopefully!) some time between when a line is prefetched into the L1I and when the line is actually first jumped to.
c-mh-v4-sof-scan-timing.notes: Handley's correction to the simple "scan at fill" reading; basic predecode does happen at fill (c-mh-v4-predecode-every-line).

c-mh-v4-sof-cloudflare.text: Reading Cloudflare's cold-predictor M1 graph, Handley sees about 8 cycles for the first fetch into a line and about 3 more for each further branch the scan-on-fill predictor supplies (about 11 for two, 17 for four)
c-mh-v4-sof-cloudflare.quote: So it looks like we always pay the fixed cost of 8 cycles, plus 3 cycles if we can extract the data from the line using the Scan on Fill Predictor.
c-mh-v4-sof-cloudflare.notes: Assumes the lines are already in the L1I ("if we assume the lines are already in L1I?"); he calls Cloudflare's own analysis "totally off".

c-mh-v4-sof-zero-bubble.text: The fetch predictor and the scan-on-fill predictor both redirect with no bubble between taken branches; Handley guesses the scan-on-fill predictor holds maybe 512-1024 entries
c-mh-v4-sof-zero-bubble.quote: Who knows how long this is (maybe 512..1024 items?) ... Both of these provide zero cycle bubbles between taken branches.
c-mh-v4-sof-zero-bubble.hedge: Who knows how long this is (maybe 512..1024 items?)

c-mh-v4-early-resteer.text: A wrong direction, indirect target or return caught by a slower predictor before rename costs about 2-5 cycles of refetch, far less than a full flush
c-mh-v4-early-resteer.quote: This will cost maybe 2..5 cycles depending on exactly where the issue is detected (which in turn depends on which Predictor wants to force a Resteer)

c-mh-v4-nfp-return-table.text: Per a 2017 patent, fetch groups ending in a return move to a separate NFP Return table storing neither target nor fetch width (the RAS supplies the target); Handley guesses it is direct-mapped
c-mh-v4-nfp-return-table.quote: any NFP entry that terminates in a Return is wasting the storage used for the Target ... Hence those entries are moved to a separate table called the NFP Return table.

c-mh-v4-nfp-usefulness.text: Entries in the primary next-fetch predictor carry usefulness bits, a hysteresis bit and target-confidence bits, used to pick the way to replace and to retarget an entry
c-mh-v4-nfp-usefulness.quote: So entries are defined by a few different “usefulness” bits. + One of these is a hysteresis bit ... + A second such is confidence bits
c-mh-v4-nfp-usefulness.notes: US10445102B1 (2017); Handley reads the two as one 2-bit counter whose start value sets how many early mispredictions an entry survives.

c-mh-v4-nfp-overflow-table.text: When both ways of a primary next-fetch-predictor set are valid and strong, the new entry goes to an overflow table (the patent's NFP Fast Table), a FIFO without usefulness bits, like a victim cache
c-mh-v4-nfp-overflow-table.quote: If both entries for a particular index in the primary Next Fetch Predictor table are valid and have high strength, then we allocate this additional entry into this overflow table

c-mh-v4-nfp-lookup-priority.text: Each cycle the PC goes to the primary NFP, the Return NFP, the overflow table and the scan-on-fill predictor; on several hits the primary NFP wins, then Return, then overflow, then scan-on-fill
c-mh-v4-nfp-lookup-priority.quote: If more than hit gets a hit, the NFP gets highest priority, then the Return NFP, then the overflow table, and finally the Scan-on-Fill table.
c-mh-v4-nfp-lookup-priority.notes: US10445102B1 (2017); hints of different behaviour under low power or high misprediction, no details.

c-mh-v4-m1-nfp-dm.text: For the M1 Handley guesses a two-level next-fetch predictor: a first level of perhaps 1024 entries, direct-mapped, and a second of at least 8192 entries, probably 2-4 way, unlike the two-way patent design
c-mh-v4-m1-nfp-dm.quote: As of the patent this was two-way set associative, tag probably gshare with recent history; As of M1, perhaps two level with L1 perhaps 1024 entries direct-mapped, and L2 at least 8192 entries, probably two, three or four way associative
c-mh-v4-m1-nfp-dm.notes: Value is the first level's associativity. Disagrees with the 2-way patent readings c-mh-v4-nfp-2way and c-mh-v4-nfp-two-tags. He elsewhere equates the second level with the L1I (c-mh-v4-btb-l1i-8192).

c-mh-v4-nfp-slices.text: Handley speculates the fetch predictor is built in slices: each row has one half for fetch groups ending in a branch (target and width) and a separately tagged half for branch-structure hints about the next groups
c-mh-v4-nfp-slices.quote: So for the Fetch Predictor, I think we have this sort of slice structure. Each row in the Fetch Predictor has - a first half that holds “Fetch Groups that will end in a branch”
c-mh-v4-nfp-slices.notes: Handley introduces it with "I'm going to out on a limb here", by analogy with his ROB rows.

c-mh-v4-l2-ilines.text: Handley expects the L2 to favour keeping instruction lines over data lines; he lists this among Apple's features, though it would not show up in patents
c-mh-v4-l2-ilines.quote: slightly prioritize I-lines in the L2 cache over D-lines ... I expect Apple is doing so
c-mh-v4-l2-ilines.hedge: I expect Apple is doing so
c-mh-v4-l2-ilines.notes: Handley lists "treating I-lines in L2 as critical so that they are retained in the cache longer than D-lines".

c-mh-v4-iprefetch-two-tables.text: Apple's more recent instruction prefetcher extends call-path prefetch (DIP-like) with TAGE-style tables of different path lengths, two so far
c-mh-v4-iprefetch-two-tables.quote: their more recent I-Prefetcher (which augments the basic DIP idea of prediction based on a path ... with an idea from TAGE (multiple, for now two, prediction tables using paths of different lengths]

c-mh-v4-callgraph-details.text: In the callgraph-prefetch patent the signature is an aging hash (shift, then XOR in each call target or return address), and each signature prefetches at most two lines, the target line and possibly the next
c-mh-v4-callgraph-details.quote: Apple seems to construct an “aging” hash where on each event (call or return) we shift the history ... Each event can only result in up to two prefetches, of the target line and possibly the target line+1.
c-mh-v4-callgraph-details.notes: Beyond c-pat-us10642618b1-callgraph-prefetch, per-line usefulness counters plus recency drive replacement, and a Bloom filter screens Miss Table lookups. Far less aggressive than RDIP.

c-mh-v4-ogehl-2012.text: Per Apple's 2012 patent, the branch direction predictor of that time was O-GEHL, a perceptron-weighted predictor combining tables of several history lengths
c-mh-v4-ogehl-2012.quote: The Branch Direction Predictor (as of 2012) was the O-GEHL version of the Perceptron predictor
c-mh-v4-ogehl-2012.notes: US20140089647A1 (2012). Superseded by the TAGE-like design (c-mh-v4-tage)

c-mh-v4-bp-confidence-retrain.text: Per the 2012 patent, each predicted branch carries a confident/weak flag and the table indices used, so the predictor is retrained on mispredictions and on correct but weak predictions, and not otherwise
c-mh-v4-bp-confidence-retrain.quote: what the Branch Predictor actually feeds forward, along with the predicted branch outcome (all attached to the Branch instruction) is ... an indication of whether the branch was confidently or weakly predicted
c-mh-v4-bp-confidence-retrain.notes: US20140089647A1 (2012). Handley suggests a lower-power variant keeps the indices in a local circular table and sends only a pointer with the branch

c-mh-v4-bp-line-rows.text: Per the 2012 patent, the direction predictor is indexed by the fetch group's cache-line address and each row holds a counter for every instruction slot in the line, so one lookup covers every branch in the fetch group
c-mh-v4-bp-line-rows.quote: with a single Fetch Group PC we can identify the appropriate row of the Branch Direction Predictor, which holds prediction data for all possible branches in that line
c-mh-v4-bp-line-rows.notes: US20140089647A1 (2012). Handley's example (128 B line, 32 counters per row, 128 rows) is illustrative. Works for the global tables too because all branches in a trace share the same path history

c-mh-v4-bp-half-banks.text: Per the 2012 patent, predictor storage is split into two halves so a fetch group spanning two lines can still read a full line's width, and the unused half is not powered when the group fits in half a line
c-mh-v4-bp-half-banks.quote: the actual storage is split into two halves, so that one can always access a full line’s width of storage

c-mh-v4-tage.text: By 2015 Apple's direction predictor is a proper TAGE-like system (patent US10719327B1): tagged tables indexed by PC and increasingly long path history, best-match selection and usefulness bits
c-mh-v4-tage.quote: By 2015 Apple have moved on to a proper TAGE-like system, but they add one interesting twist
c-mh-v4-tage.notes: Handley later calls it the M1's TAGE (c-mh-v4-m1-tage)

c-mh-v4-tage-assoc.text: Per the 2015 patent, each TAGE table may be direct-mapped, 2-way or 4-way, with ways and sets chosen per table; Handley guesses 4-way for short-history tables, 2-way for intermediate and direct-mapped for long
c-mh-v4-tage-assoc.quote: Each of the TAGE tables can be implemented not as a direct-mapped cache but as two- or four-way, with different tables having a different number of ways
c-mh-v4-tage-assoc.notes: US10719327B1 (2015); per-table associativity is the patent's novelty. Handley's nine tables and the 4/2/1-way split are his illustration

c-mh-v4-tage-sequential.text: Per the 2015 patent, the TAGE tables are probed partly in sequence rather than all in parallel to save energy; Handley imagines three groups of three tables, a later group probed only if earlier ones miss or are weak
c-mh-v4-tage-sequential.quote: to save energy, there is some degree of sequential testing of the different tables rather than full parallel testing
c-mh-v4-tage-sequential.hedge: The details are not given, but one could imagine
c-mh-v4-tage-sequential.notes: US10719327B1 (2015). Handley: not exactly TAGE's best match across all lengths, but close enough at lower power

c-mh-v4-tage-power-gating.text: Per a 2016 patent, deep power-saving modes power off TAGE tables selectively, favouring tables with few useful entries and shorter histories; a re-powered table stays off until training gives it an entry
c-mh-v4-tage-power-gating.quote: maintain a measure of how many useful values are in each of the tables ... preferentially cut power to the shorter-history tables

c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-tables.text: Per Apple's 2013 indirect predictor patent, two tables are read in parallel: a 1024-entry table indexed by a hash of path history and PC, and a 2-way PC table indexed by PC bits 5..9; a history-table hit wins
c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-tables.quote: the history table has 1024 entries (indexed by a hash of 10 bits of path data and some bits of PC data) ... the PC table has 32 entries
c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-tables.notes: US9311100B2 (2013), a cascaded predictor after Driesen and Holzle. Handley says this design "is now replaced by something like ITTAGE/COTTAGE". The PC table is described both as 32 entries and as 2-way with two entries per index

c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-training.text: Per the 2013 patent, a new indirect branch goes into the PC table if a slot is free, else the history table; a PC-table entry that mispredicts is marked not useful and a history-table entry is made for it
c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-training.quote: When a new indirect branch is encountered, the initial impulse is classify it in the PC-based predictor. ... If a branch already in the PC-based predictor mispredicts, we mark its usefulness as 0
c-mh-v4-ibp-2013-training.notes: US9311100B2 (2013). Usefulness counters also arbitrate replacement in the history table

c-mh-v4-ibp-hysteresis.text: In the 2013 indirect predictor, history-table entries carry hysteresis: an entry keeps its target after one misprediction and switches only after two in a row
c-mh-v4-ibp-hysteresis.quote: The hysteresis value allows entries in the history-based table to make one mistake while retaining the current target.
c-mh-v4-ibp-hysteresis.notes: US9311100B2 (2013); Handley calls hysteresis a common Apple feature in caches

c-mh-v4-ibp-8kb.text: Handley estimates the 2013 indirect predictor at about 1000 entries of about 8 bytes, roughly 8 KB, against the 64 KB suggested in the ITTAGE paper
c-mh-v4-ibp-8kb.quote: the size of this predictor storage is ~1000 entries, call them 8 bytes long ... So we're talking ~8kB for the indirect branch predictor
c-mh-v4-ibp-8kb.notes: Handley's own sizing of the 2013 design (6 B of target, 2 B of tag and usefulness per entry)

c-mh-v4-ibp-m1-long-history.text: The 2013 indirect predictor lacks ITTAGE-style very long branch history; Handley assumes the M1 has added it
c-mh-v4-ibp-m1-long-history.quote: missing, is sophisticated use of a very long branch history as in IT-TAGE, but I would assume that by now with the M1 that has been corrected
c-mh-v4-ibp-m1-long-history.notes: No evidence given; see c-mh-v4-ibp-ittage for the patent statement that the predictor is a TAGE variant

c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-not-m1.text: The register-operand indirect predictor for objc_msgSend (patent US20210240477A1) is not in the A14/M1
c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-not-m1.quote: This patent represents functionality that we know is not in the A14/M1
c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-not-m1.notes: Handley does not say how this is known; he links Apple's objc4 runtime header objc-bp-assist.h, which configures the hardware

c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-m2.text: The register-operand indirect predictor for objc_msgSend appears to be present in the A15/M2
c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-m2.quote: functionality that we know is not in the A14/M1, but appears to be present in the A15/M2
c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-m2.notes: Handley believes WebKit's JavaScript dispatcher also uses it

c-mh-v4-mop-pred-uop.text: Per the 2020 patent, Decode compares each BR with one configured hot PC and on a match inserts a predict uop before it; configuration registers also name two key registers, x16 (class) and x1 (selector)
c-mh-v4-mop-pred-uop.quote: Each branch-to-register (BR) instruction in Decode is compared against the special hot PC. If there’s a match, then a special fake “predict” instruction is inserted before the BR
c-mh-v4-mop-pred-uop.notes: US20210240477A1; the registers are set at app initialization. On the A15/M2, not the M1 (c-mh-v4-objc-predictor-not-m1). A fake dependency through an sts register keeps the predict uop ahead of the BR.

c-mh-v4-mop-cache.text: The predict uop hashes x16 and x1 into a roughly 10-bit index into a Method/Object Predictor (MOP) cache and redirects fetch on a hit; the MOP entry is written from a training entry when the BR retires
c-mh-v4-mop-cache.quote: create a hash from x16 (the class) and x1 (the method selector), using the usual xor’s and folding ... something like a 10-bit index, which will be looked up in the MOP (Method/Object Predictor) cache
c-mh-v4-mop-cache.notes: US20210240477A1 (2020). The MOP cache entries carry a security tag

c-mh-v4-ibp-prev-call-pc.text: Per a 2020 patent, for the configured hot indirect branch the indirect predictor indexes and tags with the PC of the previous function call instead of the branch's own PC
c-mh-v4-ibp-prev-call-pc.quote: usually we use the current PC except when that current PC equals the hot PC, in which case we use the prior PC
c-mh-v4-ibp-prev-call-pc.notes: US11294684B2 (2020). Placed on m2 since it relies on the hot-PC configuration of the objc_msgSend predictor, which Handley places on the A15/M2; he does not name a chip for this patent himself

c-mh-v4-ibp-ittage.text: Per a 2020 patent, Apple's indirect branch predictor is a TAGE variant, something like ITTAGE or COTTAGE
c-mh-v4-ibp-ittage.quote: We begin by confirming that the IBP is a TAGE variant, something like ITTAGE or COTTAGE
c-mh-v4-ibp-ittage.notes: US11294684B2 (2020). Handley says the 2013 two-table design "is now replaced by something like ITTAGE/COTTAGE"; the 2016 branch-information patent also shows TAGE elements in the indirect predictor (c-mh-v4-ibp-btp-hit)

c-mh-v4-loop-buffers-m1.text: The M1 has several kinds of loop buffer, mainly to save energy, since a loop's backward branch already costs it nothing; simpler loops get the more aggressive savings
c-mh-v4-loop-buffers-m1.quote: M1 already has that cost down to zero. Even so M1 incorporates a variety of loop buffers, mainly, but not exclusively to save energy.
c-mh-v4-loop-buffers-m1.notes: No method given; the section that follows reads Apple's 2012-2014 loop patents

c-mh-v4-loop-detect.text: Per a 2012 patent, a short backward branch starts loop detection; when the loop-back distance repeats with no branches in the body a few times (say three), the loop runs from the loop buffer; nothing is kept across encounters
c-mh-v4-loop-detect.quote: If we increment detection mode successfully enough times (say three times) then we assume we have a loop

c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-after-decode.text: In the 2012 patent the loop buffer sits after Decode and holds uops, so Decode is skipped too; later patents seem to place it before Decode, running loops from the instruction queue
c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-after-decode.quote: The loop buffer apparently lives after Decode. ... the cost of Decode can also be avoided.
c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-after-decode.notes: US9557999B2 (2012); Handley is unsure which placement later designs keep

c-mh-v4-loop-8-branches.text: The 2012 loop buffer accepts loops containing forward conditional branches whose outcomes do not change between iterations, tracking up to 8 of them by offset from the loop start; indirect branches disqualify a loop
c-mh-v4-loop-8-branches.quote: we have a table that can record up to 8 conditional branches, recording specifically how many instructions from the start of the loop till the branch
c-mh-v4-loop-8-branches.notes: US9557999B2 (2012). A misprediction flushes and marks the backward branch as not a loop for a while

c-mh-v4-fetch-one-group.text: In the fetch scheme Handley describes for Apple's cores, only one fetch group (a run of instructions ending at a taken branch) is fetched per cycle, so a 3-instruction loop runs at most 3 instructions per cycle
c-mh-v4-fetch-one-group.quote: only one Fetch Group (ie trace of instructions up to a taken branch) is acquired per cycle
c-mh-v4-fetch-one-group.notes: Consistent with fetch.taken_per_cycle = 1; Handley states it as a property of the scheme, not a measurement

c-mh-v4-loop-packing.text: Per a 2012 patent, a short loop body is replicated in the loop buffer as many times as fits, so dispatch is not limited to one iteration (one fetch group) per cycle
c-mh-v4-loop-packing.quote: the loop body will be replicated in the buffer as many times as will fit. This bypasses the Fetch limit.
c-mh-v4-loop-packing.notes: US9753733B2 (2012). Dispatch from the buffer is "6 at a time in 2012, 8 at a time now". Neither 2012 patent says how the loop is exited other than by a misprediction

c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-96.text: The 2012 loop-packing patent suggests a loop buffer of 16 rows of 6 slots, about 96 uops, matching the 6-wide decode of A7-class cores
c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-96.quote: arranged as 16 rows of 6 slots (6 slots because decode for that generation of A7-class CPUs had 6-wide decode); so able to hold about 96 ops
c-mh-v4-loop-buffer-96.notes: US9753733B2 (2012), A7 generation; no M1 loop-buffer size is given. Handley compares Skylake's 64-uop IDQ

c-mh-v4-l0-cache.text: Per a 2014 patent, instructions can come from four sources: normal fetch with the I-cache and full predictors, a small L0 cache (probably direct mapped) sequenced by a simple local predictor, a loop buffer, and a trace cache
c-mh-v4-l0-cache.quote: an L0 cache (smaller and lower power than the I cache, probably direct mapped)
c-mh-v4-l0-cache.notes: US20150205725A1 (2014). The L0 serves loops with mostly predictable internal branches that fail the loop-buffer tests; Handley guesses its predictor is gshare-like. No details on when the trace cache is used

c-mh-v4-l0-size.text: The L0 size is not given; other patents suggest it is about the size of the loop buffer, itself about the size of the fetch queue: maybe 8 to 12 lines of 16 instructions
c-mh-v4-l0-size.quote: it’s much the same size as the Loop Buffer, which is much the same size as the Fetch Queue; so maybe 8 to 12 lines each holding 16 instructions, something like that
c-mh-v4-l0-size.notes: Range 8-12 lines of 16 instructions; value is the midpoint. Bears on iq.depth (the fetch queue), but is a guess stated in lines

c-mh-v4-loop-table.text: Per a 2014 patent, a previous-loop table records each loop's start, end and iteration count and the kinds and variability of the branches in its body, and updates itself when these change
c-mh-v4-loop-table.quote: a “previous loop table” has now been added to the system. This table records some obvious things like the loop, start, end, and iteration count
c-mh-v4-loop-table.notes: US9524011B2 (2014). Unclear whether the table holds several loops or several branches of one nested loop, or whether it is used on later encounters

c-mh-v4-loop-iq-mode.text: Per the 2014 tiered patent, after two or three iterations a loop runs from the instruction queue with fetch and the I-cache asleep but direction prediction awake; after about 20 iterations it may move to the loop buffer or L0
c-mh-v4-loop-iq-mode.quote: This puts Fetch and the I-cache to sleep (but Branch Direction Prediction stays awake) and we run the loop out of the Instruction Queue
c-mh-v4-loop-iq-mode.notes: US9524011B2 (2014). Loop mode starts "perhaps after just two or three iterations". To enter it, fetch must force the loop body into the instruction queue instead of bypassing it to Decode

c-mh-v4-loop-exit-predictor.text: Per a 2014 patent, while a loop runs from the loop buffer or L0 the direction predictor stays on to predict the exit until branch history saturates; loops whose exit keeps mispredicting turn it off from the start
c-mh-v4-loop-exit-predictor.quote: we keep the Branch Direction Predictor alive, to (hopefully) predict the exit condition ... for as long we have not saturated the Branch History vectors
c-mh-v4-loop-exit-predictor.notes: US9471322B2 (2014). Per-loop state is kept in an Early Loop Buffer Mode Table

c-mh-v4-bit-tables.text: A Branch Information Table and a Taken Branch Information Table hold each branch's predictor state (RAS top of stack, path histories, targets) from Decode to Retire; at retirement it is sent to the predictors for training
c-mh-v4-bit-tables.quote: there are two large subtables, the BIT and the TBIT (Taken Branch Information Table) each with subsections for different types of branch
c-mh-v4-bit-tables.notes: Detailed from US10175982B1 (2016) in c-mh-v4-bit-60 and c-mh-v4-tbit-96

c-mh-v4-ras-two.text: Per Apple's 2011 RAS patent, there are two return stacks, a small speculative RAS used by fetch and an Execution RAS kept as a linked list, against about five in Intel's design
c-mh-v4-ras-two.quote: So Apple have one for Fetch, and another that's modified at Execution. In particular the Execution RAS (implemented in the linked list form)
c-mh-v4-ras-two.notes: US9354886B2 (2011). The patent's speculative RAS is Handley's MiniRAS. A "first time" bit in the BIT keeps load replay of RET or BR from pushing or popping the Execution RAS twice; the 2013 redesign supersedes this

c-mh-v4-ras-linked-guess.text: Handley's guess: the Execution RAS is a pure linked list in an array of perhaps 90 entries with valid bits, an entry freed when its RET retires, so overflow comes only from very deep call nesting
c-mh-v4-ras-linked-guess.quote: treat the structure as a pure linked list, implemented with a finite array of node-sized entries (say 90 or so), where each entry has a “valid” bit
c-mh-v4-ras-linked-guess.hedge: Here's my guess as to what Apple does
c-mh-v4-ras-linked-guess.notes: "say 90 or so" is illustrative, the size of a node array in a guessed implementation, not a return-stack depth (cf. the 50-entry return stack, c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50). Handley: "we're already on such a limb"

c-mh-v4-ras-at-decode.text: Per a 2013 patent, the main RAS is maintained at Decode, pushed on calls and popped on returns there, so load replay no longer threatens it
c-mh-v4-ras-at-decode.quote: the main RAS (what was previously called the Execution RAS) is now maintained at Decode rather than at Execute
c-mh-v4-ras-at-decode.notes: US9405544B2 (2013), described by Handley as a 2014 design

c-mh-v4-ras-mini.text: In the 2013 design the fetch-side MiniRAS only covers returns that follow calls not yet seen by Decode, tracked by call and return counts between Fetch and Decode, so it is much smaller than the main RAS
c-mh-v4-ras-mini.quote: The MiniRAS is only required if there is a return following a very recent call, so that that the call has not yet propagated to the primary RAS

c-mh-v4-predecode-call-ret.text: Predecode bits mark calls and returns, so for lines not yet in the fetch predictor, fetch takes a return's target from the MiniRAS and pauses after a call until a predictor or execution supplies the target
c-mh-v4-predecode-call-ret.quote: from the predecode bits, it will know that the Fetch Group it is sending downstream includes a call or a return

c-mh-v4-pac-ras.text: Per a 2016 patent, pointer authentication codes in the high bits of return addresses are checked as part of the logic that reads and writes the RAS
c-mh-v4-pac-ras.quote: PAC (Pointer Authentication) stuff that encodes the 2015 tag in a few high bits of the return address ... always checked as part of logic that reads and writes the RAS
c-mh-v4-pac-ras.notes: US10409600B1 (2016). The 2015 forerunner (US10867031B2) used a RAS misprediction to trigger call/return tag checks; Handley is not sure it was ever built

c-mh-v4-bp-security-tag.text: Handley reads the 2018 predictor-security patent as adding a security tag (protection level, process ID, VM ID, high PC bits) to predictor entries; if it does not match the machine state, the prediction is not used
c-mh-v4-bp-security-tag.quote: augment that tag with a security tag which holds, among other things, the protection level, the process ID, the VM ID, and some of the high bits of the PC
c-mh-v4-bp-security-tag.notes: US20200192673A1; the patent's own claim is c-pat-us20200192673a1-context-encrypted-targets. Handley says such a tag "is in fact implemented to some extent", and high PC bits can separate JIT code from its host.

c-mh-v4-predecode-offset.text: Per a 2014 patent, predecode on I-cache fill stores the low 14 bits (page offset) of each PC-relative branch target, so only the upper bits are added at use and a target lookup can start at once, safe under aliasing
c-mh-v4-predecode-offset.quote: Suppose that rather than calculating the entire target address we calculate only the lowest fourteen bits.
c-mh-v4-predecode-offset.notes: US9940262B2 (2014). Full targets would break when a physically tagged line is shared by processes that map a library at different virtual addresses

c-mh-v4-predecode-undef.text: Per a 2014 patent, predecode replaces every undefined instruction encoding with a single undefined value, so Decode checks for only one
c-mh-v4-predecode-undef.quote: replace them with a single "undefined instruction" value

c-mh-v4-seq-line-power.text: Per a 2010 patent, the ITLB and tag lookups are skipped when sequential fetch reads from the same I-cache line as in the previous cycle
c-mh-v4-seq-line-power.quote: suppresses the ITLB and tags lookup in the case where sequential Fetch reads instructions from the same I-cache line as was accessed in the previous cycle

c-mh-v4-seq-way-pred.text: Per a 2013 patent, a sequential way predictor gives the I-cache ways of the next few sequential lines from a fetch PC, so only those ways are precharged and tag lookups are skipped
c-mh-v4-seq-way-pred.quote: Way Predictor that, when given a Fetch PC, gives the way information for say the next four sequen-tial cache lines
c-mh-v4-seq-way-pred.notes: US9311098B2 (2013). Handley guesses the last ITLB translation is held in a register in Fetch to skip the TLB too

c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-gating.text: Per a 2013 patent, fetch-predictor entries record which kinds of branch the next fetch group contains, so the conditional, indirect and return predictors can be clock-gated when not needed
c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-gating.quote: since the Fetch Predictor contains information about whether the next Fetch Group contains conditional branches, indirect calls, and returns
c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-gating.notes: US10901484B2 (2013). Handley says the patent's details may be obsolete relative to the M1

c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-split.text: In Handley's reading of the same patent, the fetch predictor is two PC-indexed arrays, one for groups ending in a taken branch (with target) and one for fall-through groups, letting predictors sleep two or three groups ahead
c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-split.quote: the Fetch Predictor array is split into two pieces. They are both indexed by the current PC
c-mh-v4-fetch-pred-split.hedge: I think what they are trying to say is

c-mh-v4-fetch-bitmaps.text: The fetch prediction unit keeps two bitmaps over the I-cache lines, recording whether a line's tag and TLB result are held in the fetch predictor and whether the line has changed, so tag and ITLB lookups can be skipped
c-mh-v4-fetch-bitmaps.quote: the Fetch Prediction Unit holds two bitmaps of every line of the I-cache

c-mh-v4-subroutine-power.text: Per a 2016 patent, on a call fetch reads the whole line's predecode bits and stores them in the RAS, so after the return the conditional and indirect predictors can be clock-gated and the fetch width set
c-mh-v4-subroutine-power.quote: load the entire line’s worth of pre-decode bits ... We can store this information in the Return Address Stack
c-mh-v4-subroutine-power.notes: US10203959B1 (2016); helps only for calls not already held in the predictors

c-mh-v4-m1-tage.text: Handley calls the M1's main direction predictor a TAGE system and suggests a small companion loop predictor so TAGE could be shut down soon after loop mode starts
c-mh-v4-m1-tage.quote: a nice, small, companion predictor for the primary M1 TAGE system
c-mh-v4-m1-tage.notes: Aside in the fetch summary; rests on the patent reading in c-mh-v4-tage, no measurement

c-mh-v4-nfp-contents.text: The Next Fetch Predictor (Apple's BTB) is a cache indexed by the previous fetch PC that returns the next trace: target PC, length, energy data such as TLB result and I-cache way, maybe a return marker
c-mh-v4-nfp-contents.quote: The NFP (ie the Next Fetch Predictor, ie what everyone else calls the BTB) is a cache. The index used for lookup is the previous PC

c-mh-v4-nfp-assoc.text: The Next Fetch Predictor has been something like 512 sets of 2 ways, perhaps 256 sets of 4 ways in future
c-mh-v4-nfp-assoc.quote: In the past something like 512 sets each of 2 ways; maybe in future 256 sets each of 4 ways?
c-mh-v4-nfp-assoc.notes: "In the past" names no chip, and no source or method is given. Handley adds that Apple may prefer 2 ways (lower power) where others use 4, with set index from the low 9 PC bits and about 10 tag bits, probably hashed with the ASID

c-mh-v4-checkpoints.text: Apple probably adds checkpoints to the History File for faster misprediction recovery; a 2013 patent refers to them, but no details are known
c-mh-v4-checkpoints.quote: It’s probable that Apple uses these, and we have a patent from 2013 that refers to them, but no further details.
c-mh-v4-checkpoints.notes: US9311084B2 (2013, RDA checkpoint optimization); the RDA itself has since been replaced

c-mh-v4-not-taken-untrained.text: Predicted-not-taken branches are meant to be almost NOPs: always-not-taken branches never enter the predictor tables, and finding no prediction means predicting not taken
c-mh-v4-not-taken-untrained.quote: if a not-taken branch is encountered, I think we don't bother training on it
c-mh-v4-not-taken-untrained.notes: Handley guesses this holds for about half of branches, saving table space and training effort

c-mh-v4-bit-60.text: The example in Apple's 2016 branch-information patent has a 60-entry BIT, a circular queue allocated at Decode for every branch and holding pending branches between allocation and retirement
c-mh-v4-bit-60.quote: in the example given in the patent, they suggest the BIT holds 60 entries, while the TBIT holds 96 entries
c-mh-v4-bit-60.notes: US10175982B1 (2016), example values only. Handley does not know the current sizes or whether the structures still exist in this form

c-mh-v4-tbit-96.text: The same patent example has a 96-entry TBIT, allocated for predicted-taken branches (or at execute for mispredicted not-taken ones); Handley reads the extra 36 entries as retired branches still awaiting predictor training
c-mh-v4-tbit-96.quote: in the example given in the patent, they suggest the BIT holds 60 entries, while the TBIT holds 96 entries
c-mh-v4-tbit-96.notes: US10175982B1 (2016), example values only. BIT slices: all branches, conditional; TBIT slices: indirect, all taken, call/return, with the BIT conditional slice and TBIT indirect slice sharing entry size

c-mh-v4-path-histories.text: The 2016 patent keeps two path histories, GHIST (shifted one bit and XORed with each taken branch's target) and PHIST (shifted one bit and XORed with 4 bits of the branch PC), and no direction history
c-mh-v4-path-histories.quote: The GHIST vector is the “target path history” vector, created by, on taken branches ... xor’ing in 4 bits of new branch PC
c-mh-v4-path-histories.notes: US10175982B1 (2016). Gives no history length. Handley expects such details (4 bits, update only on taken branches) to have changed since

c-mh-v4-ibp-btp-hit.text: The 2016 patent's fields show the indirect predictor using TAGE elements (multiple tables, usefulness bits) plus a BTP hit table, probably to power the predictor down when it is rarely used
c-mh-v4-ibp-btp-hit.quote: They suggest that the Indirect Branch Predictor uses elements of TAGE (like multiple tables and U bits), as expected, but also add a “BTP hit table”

c-mh-v4-bit-overwrite.text: Per the 2016 patent, a full BIT or TBIT does not stall the core: older entries are overwritten because they only serve predictor training, so a long run of not-taken branches may show no BIT limit
c-mh-v4-bit-overwrite.quote: if one of the tables ever becomes full, the machinery should just keep going overwriting older entries
c-mh-v4-bit-overwrite.notes: US10175982B1 (2016). Handley's point is that a not-taken-branch probe for the BIT size might not work

c-mh-v4-iq-bypass.text: Fetch draws from up to two cache lines per cycle; fetched instructions go straight to Decode when the instruction queue is empty and into the queue otherwise, possibly split between both in one cycle
c-mh-v4-iq-bypass.quote: Fetch has to pull in some number of instructions from up to two cache lines ... if the Instruction Queue is empty, then the Fetch’ed instructions should be delivered directly to Decode without buffering
c-mh-v4-iq-bypass.notes: US10445091B1 (2016), which Handley says describes the A6. Its improvement treats the fetch buffer as a circular buffer to cut mux logic

c-mh-v4-cold-start-fetch.text: Per a 2016 patent, after a cold start (power-up with empty caches) instruction fetch from the L2 turns aggressive, each one-line fetch becoming three lines
c-mh-v4-cold-start-fetch.quote: during the aggressive phase of a cold start, replacing each fetch of a single line from the L2 with three lines

c-mh-v4-cold-start-tage.text: In the same cold-start phase a new branch is written into four TAGE entries instead of the usual one or two, while the tables hold little useful data
c-mh-v4-cold-start-tage.quote: during the aggressive phase of a cold start ... four (rather than two or one) TAGE entries

c-mh-v4-prefetch-boost.text: Per a 2017 patent, the L1 instruction and data prefetchers turn more aggressive when demand or prefetch misses take longer than expected to return (missing in L2 or the SLC)
c-mh-v4-prefetch-boost.quote: the L1 prefetcher monitors whether demand or prefetch misses take longer than expected to return
c-mh-v4-prefetch-boost.notes: US10346309B1 (2017). Handley's queue sizes (64 entries, 12/32/64 active) are explicitly made up; he thinks Apple does not yet have a decoupled prefetch-address engine

c-mh-v4-decode-8.quote: Each Decoder (so 8 as of M1) is a block that consists of a few sub-decoders
c-mh-v4-decode-8.notes: Aside with no method; Handley's own measurement of the 8-wide front end is in vol 1 (c-mh-v1-frontend-8)

c-mh-v4-decode-vector-gating.text: Per a 2010 patent, each decoder has integer, load/store, vector-integer and vector-FP sub-decoders; the vector ones stay gated off until needed, woken by a small table of vector PCs and kept awake by a timer
c-mh-v4-decode-vector-gating.quote: the instruction to be decoded is fed directly to the Integer and Load/Store decoders, but is usually blocked from going to the Vector Decoders
c-mh-v4-decode-vector-gating.notes: US20120079249A1 (2010, Swift era). A vector instruction that finds its decoder asleep loops round for another pass, costing at least a cycle

c-mh-v4-trace-length.text: Because the fetch predictor skips expected-not-taken branches, the average fetched trace is around 10 instructions, an adequate but tight match for 8 instructions per cycle
c-mh-v4-trace-length.quote: which means that the average length of a trace is around 10 instructions or so

c-mh-v4-iq-fixup.text: Apple appears to fix up fetch predictions in the instruction queue using the slower predictors, but not to drop short forward branches from the fetch predictor or convert them to predicated instructions
c-mh-v4-iq-fixup.quote: Apple appear to have some elements of this scheme (if possible, fixup predictions from slow branch predictors in the Instruction Queue) in place
c-mh-v4-iq-fixup.notes: A mispredicted short forward branch can be fixed by marking its instructions in the instruction queue invalid, without resteering fetch

c-dj-width.text: Firestorm's pipeline width is eight instructions (uops) per cycle
c-dj-width.quote: Firestorm has a pipeline width of eight instructions per cycle. Uops per cycle: 8
c-dj-width.notes: Johnson gives one pipeline width, not separate fetch/decode/rename widths. Method from #firestorm-pipeline-overview (uops counted with the RETIRE_UOP counter against the 8 uops/cycle limit).

c-dj-taken.text: Firestorm sustains one taken branch per cycle
c-dj-taken.quote: Uops per cycle: 8 Taken branches per cycle: 1
c-dj-taken.notes: The page does not say how this was measured.

c-dj-int-prf.text: The integer physical register file holds about 380 to 394 registers
c-dj-int-prf.quote: Integer physical register file size: ~380-394? ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-int-prf.notes: Johnson gives the range ~380-394 with a question mark; value is the midpoint.

c-dj-fp-prf.text: The FP/SIMD physical register file holds about 432 registers
c-dj-fp-prf.quote: FP/SIMD physical register file size: ~432? ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-flags-prf.text: The flags physical register file holds about 128 registers
c-dj-flags-prf.quote: Flags physical register file size: ~128 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-branches.text: About 144 branches can be in flight
c-dj-branches.quote: In-flight branches: ~144 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-loads.text: About 130 loads can be in flight
c-dj-loads.quote: In-flight loads: ~130 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-loads.notes: The page points to the load/store queue blog post for detail (see c-dj-lsq-lq-130).

c-dj-stores.text: About 60 stores can be in flight
c-dj-stores.quote: In-flight stores: ~60 These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-stores.notes: The page points to the load/store queue blog post for detail (see c-dj-lsq-sq-60).

c-dj-retire-groups.text: The coalesced retire queue holds about 330 retire groups
c-dj-retire-groups.quote: The coalesced retire queue consists of ~330 such groups.
c-dj-retire-groups.notes: The page names no filler; the LSQ post reaches this limit with ~329 loads or stores under an FSQRT delay (c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329). Group boundaries are c-dj-group-boundaries.

c-dj-group-size.text: A retire group may contain up to seven uops
c-dj-group-size.quote: Firestorm coalesces uops into retire groups, which all retire together. A retire group may contain up to seven uops.
c-dj-group-size.notes: Seven-uop groups are only observed for eliminated instructions (c-dj-group-issuing).

c-dj-nop-window.text: The coalesced retire queue allows an out-of-order window of over 2200 nop instructions
c-dj-nop-window.quote: This allows an out-of-order window of ... or over 2200 nop instructions.

c-dj-issuing-window.text: The coalesced retire queue allows an out-of-order window of just over 1000 contrived instructions that issue
c-dj-issuing-window.quote: This allows an out-of-order window of just over 1000 (contrived) instructions that issue

c-dj-rename-retire.text: The rename retire queue allows up to about 623 renames in flight
c-dj-rename-retire.quote: This is tracked in a separate structure, called the "rename retire queue", which allows for up to ~623 renames.
c-dj-rename-retire.notes: The every-write-needs-an-entry rule is c-dj-rename-cost. Also listed in #other-limits as "In-flight renames: ~623".

c-dj-retire-rate.text: Retirement is measured at up to eight coalesced retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-retire-rate.quote: Retirement-rate is measured at up to eight coalesced retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-retire-rate.notes: The page says "measured" but not how.

c-dj-rename-rate.text: Retirement is measured at up to sixteen rename retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-rename-rate.quote: or up to sixteen rename retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-rename-rate.notes: The page says "measured" but not how.

c-dj-int-units.text: Firestorm has six integer units (1 to 6), each with ALU and ubfm/sbfm
c-dj-int-units.quote: Integer units: 1: alu + ubfm/sbfm + flags + branch ... 6: alu + ubfm/sbfm + mul + madd + crc + bfm/extr
c-dj-int-units.notes: The page says issues are measured with SCHEDULE_UOP and per-class issue counters. Unit roles are c-dj-int-roles.

c-dj-ls-units.text: Firestorm has four load/store units handling up to 128-bit accesses: unit 7 store and AMX, unit 8 load/store and AMX, units 9 and 10 load only
c-dj-ls-units.quote: Load/store units (up to 128-bit loads and stores ... 7: store + amx 8: load/store + amx 9: load 10: load

c-dj-fp-units.text: Firestorm has four FP/SIMD units (11 to 14)
c-dj-fp-units.quote: SIMD units: 11: fp/simd 12: fp/simd 13: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr 14: fp/simd
c-dj-fp-units.notes: Unit roles are c-dj-fp-roles. For unit 14 the page lists reciprocal and reciprocal-square-root estimates (frecpe, frsqrte, urecpe, ursqrte), not fsqrt.

c-dj-mov-elim.text: 64-bit register moves (mov x0, x1) are usually handled by renaming; mov w0, w1, mov x0, xzr and adr/adrp are not eliminated
c-dj-mov-elim.quote: mov x0, x1 (usually handled by renaming, 64-bit version only) ... not eliminated, including adr/adrp, mov w0, w1 and mov x0, xzr

c-dj-zero-idiom.text: mov x0, #0 (and its 32-bit form) and movi v0.16b, #0 (and other types) are handled by renaming
c-dj-zero-idiom.quote: mov x0, #0 (handled by renaming, as is 32-bit version) ... movi v0.16b, #0 (handled by renaming, including other types)
c-dj-zero-idiom.notes: mov x0, xzr is not eliminated (c-dj-mov-elim).

c-dj-mov-imm.text: Immediate moves (mov x0, #imm, 32- and 64-bit, including bitwise/movz/movn aliases) are handled by renaming at most twice per eight instructions
c-dj-mov-imm.quote: mov x0, #123 (handled by renaming at a max of 2 per 8 instructions, both 32-bit and 64-bit. Includes all tested immediate "mov" aliases e.g. bitwise/movz/movn)

c-dj-fusion.text: Certain consecutive instruction pairs issue as one uop: flag-setting ALU + b.cc, ALU + cbz/cbnz, aese + aesmc, aesd + aesimc, aese/aesd + eor, pmull + eor, and amx + amx
c-dj-fusion.quote: Certain instructions are able to issue as one uop if they appear consecutively in the instruction stream.
c-dj-fusion.value: flag-ALU+b.cc, ALU+cbz/cbnz, aese+aesmc, aesd+aesimc, aes+eor, pmull+eor, amx+amx
c-dj-fusion.notes: Conditions and non-fused pairs: c-dj-fusion-read-limit, c-dj-fusion-cbz, c-dj-fusion-crypto, c-dj-fusion-amx, c-dj-fusion-branch-limits and c-dj-no-fusion.

c-dj-l1d-latency.text: A load's result can feed the base address of another load with 3-cycle latency
c-dj-l1d-latency.quote: Loads may be passed to the base address of other loads with 3c latency (which is nice for linked lists)
c-dj-l1d-latency.notes: The 4c ALU-chain latency is c-dj-load-alu-latency. The page gives no method for latencies.

c-dj-pipeline-flow.text: Instructions decode to one or more uops, which are mapped, renamed and placed in a dispatch queue, then dispatched to a scheduler, issue when their operands are ready, and are marked completed in the reorder buffer, which releases entries in order
c-dj-pipeline-flow.quote: Typically, an instruction is decoded to one or more uops, each uop is mapped and renamed and placed into a dispatch queue. These uops are then dispatched from the queue to a scheduler.

c-dj-issue-counters.text: Issues are counted by the documented SCHEDULE_UOP counter, and three undocumented counters count issues to the integer, load/store and SIMD units separately; uops are counted by RETIRE_UOP
c-dj-issue-counters.quote: can be measured using the documented SCHEDULE_UOP counter. Three undocumented counters measure issues to the integer, load/store, and simd units separately

c-dj-unit-issue-limit.text: Each execution unit accepts one issue per cycle
c-dj-unit-issue-limit.quote: Issues count towards the "execution unit" limits (one issue per unit per cycle)

c-dj-fewer-issues.text: Most instructions issue once per uop, but nop, ldp and fused instructions have fewer issues than uops
c-dj-fewer-issues.quote: most instructions have the same number of issues as uops, but some have fewer (e.g. nop, ldp, and fused instructions)

c-dj-shift-extend-issues.text: ALU operations with an optional shift or extend have more issues than uops
c-dj-shift-extend-issues.quote: some instructions have more issues than uops, e.g ALU operations with an optional shift or extend

c-dj-issue-peak.text: Because shifted/extended ALU ops issue more than once per uop, Firestorm can sustain 11 issues per cycle in contrived cases
c-dj-issue-peak.quote: which allows Firestorm to sustain 11 issues per cycle in contrived cases

c-dj-int-roles.text: All six integer units do ALU and ubfm/sbfm; units 1-3 set flags; 1 and 2 take branches, adr and msr/mrs nzcv; 1 also mrs; 2 indirect branches and pointer authentication; 3 and 4 probably moves from SIMD/FP; 5 and 6 multiply; 5 divide; 6 madd, crc and bfm/extr
c-dj-int-roles.quote: 1: alu + ubfm/sbfm + flags + branch ... indirect branch + ptrauth ... mov-from-simd/fp? ... 5: alu + ubfm/sbfm + mul + div 6: ... mul + madd + crc + bfm/extr
c-dj-int-roles.value: 1-6 alu, ubfm/sbfm; 1-3 flags; 1-2 branch, adr, msr/mrs nzcv; 1 mrs; 2 indirect branch, ptrauth; 3-4 mov-from-simd/fp?; 5-6 mul; 5 div; 6 madd, crc, bfm/extr

c-dj-fp-roles.text: All four SIMD units do FP/SIMD; units 13 and 14 add fcsel and moves to GPRs; unit 14 alone adds fcmp/fcmpe, fdiv, frecpe, frsqrte, fjcvtzs, ursqrte, urecpe and sha
c-dj-fp-roles.quote: 13: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr 14: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr + fcmp/e + fdiv + frecpe + frsqrte + fjcvtzs + ursqrte + urecpe + sha
c-dj-fp-roles.value: 11-14 fp/simd; 13-14 fcsel, to-gpr; 14 fcmp/e, fdiv, frecpe, frsqrte, fjcvtzs, ursqrte, urecpe, sha

c-dj-agu-shift.text: Load/store address generation includes register shifts up to LSL #3
c-dj-agu-shift.quote: Load/store units (up to 128-bit loads and stores, including address generation with shifts up to LSL #3)

c-dj-fusion-read-limit.text: Flag-setting ALU ops (adds/subs/ands/cmp/tst) fuse with a following b.cc; fusion is complete only when the fused instructions read no more than 4 registers per 6 instructions
c-dj-fusion-read-limit.quote: adds/subs/ands/cmp/tst + b.cc (complete fusion when fused instructions read no more than 4 registers per 6 instructions)

c-dj-fusion-cbz.text: ALU ops (add/sub/and/orr/eor/bic etc., including flag-setting variants) usually fuse with a following cbz/cbnz when their destination is the cbz operand
c-dj-fusion-cbz.quote: add/sub/and/orr/eor/bic/etc. + cbnz/cbz (usually fused, if destination matches cbz operand. also works with instruction variants that set flags)

c-dj-fusion-crypto.text: aese + aesmc, aesd + aesimc, aese/aesd + eor and pmull + eor usually fuse when the second instruction overwrites the first's destination in a matching operand pattern
c-dj-fusion-crypto.quote: aese + aesmc (usually fused if operands match pattern "A, B ; A, A") ... pmull + eor (usually fused if operands match pattern "A, B, C ; A, A, D" or "A, B, C ; A, D, A")

c-dj-fusion-amx.text: Pairs of AMX instructions fuse, except AMX loads and stores, probably into something like an stp
c-dj-fusion-amx.quote: amx + amx (excluding loads and stores - probably fuses to something like a stp)

c-dj-fusion-branch-limits.text: Branch fusion does not happen with implicit shift or extend, nor with instructions that read flags such as adc
c-dj-fusion-branch-limits.quote: Branch fusion does not work with implicit shift or extend, nor instructions that read flags (like adc)

c-dj-no-fusion.text: adrp + add, mov + movk, mul + umulh and udiv + msub are not fused
c-dj-no-fusion.quote: Other tested patterns are not fused, including adrp + add, mov + movk, mul + umulh, and udiv + msub.

c-dj-vec-mov-elim.text: Full-width vector register moves (mov v0.16b, v1.16b, also v0.8h etc.) are usually handled by renaming; v0.8b moves are not
c-dj-vec-mov-elim.quote: mov v0.16b, v1.16b (usually handled by renaming. Includes other full-width types e.g. v0.8h but not v0.8b)

c-dj-nop-b-no-issue.text: nop and unconditional b never issue
c-dj-nop-b-no-issue.quote: Certain instructions do not need to issue: ... nop (never issues) b (unconditional branch never issues)

c-dj-load-alu-latency.text: When a load is chained with ALU operations instead of feeding another load's base address, its latency is 4 cycles
c-dj-load-alu-latency.quote: Loads may be passed to the base address of other loads with 3c latency ... but chaining with ALU operations gives a latency of 4c.

c-dj-ldp-second-dest.text: The second destination register of an LDP always has 4-cycle latency
c-dj-ldp-second-dest.quote: (Although the second destination register in an LDP always has 4c latency.)

c-dj-index-shift-penalty.text: A load takes one extra cycle when its index register comes from a shift-like instruction; addition and bitwise producers carry no penalty
c-dj-index-shift-penalty.quote: Loads may have an extra 1-cycle of latency when the index register is the output of a shift-like instruction. Addition and bitwise operations do not have this penalty.
c-dj-index-shift-penalty.notes: Johnson says other latency chains had not been tested.

c-dj-madd-acc-latency.text: A MADD result feeds the addend of a following MADD with 1-cycle latency, but has 3-cycle latency into other instructions
c-dj-madd-acc-latency.quote: MADD's output can be passed to its third operand (the addend) with 1c latency, but if it's chained with other instructions it has 3c latency.

c-dj-int-simd-roundtrip.text: An integer-to-SIMD/FP-and-back round trip can take as little as 7 cycles, for example when chaining flags operations
c-dj-int-simd-roundtrip.quote: Integer to SIMD/FP roundtrip latency can be as low as 7c (e.g. when chaining flags operations).

c-dj-rob-model.text: Firestorm's reorder buffer is unconventional: a ~330-entry coalesced retire queue of retire groups plus a ~623-entry rename retire queue
c-dj-rob-model.quote: Firestorm uses an unconventional reorder buffer, which I described as a ~330 entry "coalesced retire queue" and a ~623 "rename retire queue"
c-dj-rob-model.value: coalesced retire queue + rename retire queue

c-dj-reclaim-table.text: Johnson equates the ~623-entry rename retire queue with a Physical Register Reclaim Table
c-dj-reclaim-table.quote: a ~623 "rename retire queue" (equivalent to a "Physical Register Reclaim Table")

c-dj-group-boundaries.text: Uops that can fail before retiring (such as memory accesses) must start a retire group, and uops that can fail after retiring (such as conditional branches) must end one
c-dj-group-boundaries.quote: Uops which can fail before retiring (such as memory accesses) must appear at the start of a group, and uops that can fail after retiring (such as conditional branches) must appear at the end of a group.

c-dj-ooo-commit.text: Non-speculative loads and stores may commit out of order, before retirement; once a store has completed, the architectural state must have advanced past it
c-dj-ooo-commit.quote: loads and stores may commit out-of-order if they are non-speculative. This has some interesting implications. In particular, once a store has "completed", the architectural state must have advanced past that point.
c-dj-ooo-commit.notes: Johnson refers to his load/store queue blog post for the evidence.

c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.text: Load and store queue entries are allocated when the ops issue from the scheduler, not at rename or dispatch
c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.quote: discovered that load and store queue entries are allocated when the ops issue from the scheduler
c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.notes: Intro, before the first heading. Reasoning in #final-notes: the 58-instruction gap between loads+loads and fsqrts+loads means loads keep entering the scheduler after the queue is full, "So I conclude that the resources are allocated late."

c-dj-lsq-lq-130.text: With two cache-missing loads as the delay, 128 loads fit between them before a stall; counting both delay loads, the load queue holds 130 entries
c-dj-lsq-lq-130.quote: Since the first load, 128 other loads, and the last load are in flight at the same time, I'd call this a load queue size of 130
c-dj-lsq-lq-130.notes: Delay: two independent cache-missing loads; filler: loads. Johnson: "I still believe this to be correct". The FSQRT + dependent-branch probe gives 188 = 130 + 58 (c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188).

c-dj-lsq-store-107.text: With cache-missing loads as the delay, 107 stores fit between them before a stall; Johnson withdrew his earlier reading of this as a 107-entry store queue
c-dj-lsq-store-107.quote: 128 loads or 107 stores could run, without stopping the final long-latency load from executing in parallel ... I incorrectly called this a 107 entry store queue.
c-dj-lsq-store-107.notes: Delay: two cache-missing loads; filler: stores. Explained as 60 store-queue entries plus 47 scheduler entries (c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47); the base-register effect is c-dj-lsq-x29-base.

c-dj-lsq-sched-48.quote: the load/store scheduler has 48 entries ... I found the last point at which an independent load could still fit into the scheduler and run, to find the scheduler size.
c-dj-lsq-sched-48.filler: loads or stores with addresses dependent on the delay
c-dj-lsq-sched-48.notes: Delay: a long-latency chain; filler: loads or stores whose addresses depend on it; probe: one independent load that still runs. Repeated in #fighting-stores-with-square-roots.

c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.text: The load/store dispatch queue in front of the scheduler has 10 entries
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.quote: with a 10 entry dispatch queue ... the number of extra load/stores, once the scheduler was full, that were required to block independent floating-point operations. That gives the dispatch queue size.
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.filler: loads or stores with addresses dependent on the delay
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.notes: Delay: a long-latency chain; filler: dependent loads/stores beyond a full scheduler; probe: independent FP ops that get blocked. Mixing op types separates the queues.

c-dj-lsq-dispatch-stall.text: An op that finds both its scheduler and its dispatch queue full stalls the frontend: no further ops enter any dispatch queue until that queue has room
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-stall.quote: But if the scheduler and dispatch queue are full, and we have an op that needs to go to that queue, we stall. This means no more ops can enter any dispatch queues until there is room in that queue.

c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.text: With chains of square roots as the delay, about 329 loads or stores fit between them, the same limit for mixed loads and stores; Johnson attributes it to the coalescing retire queue, not the load/store queues
c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.quote: about 329 loads or stores can run between floating point operations, without forcing the two long-latency chains to run completely in parallel
c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.notes: Delay: long-latency FP chains (fsqrt, per the heading and #final-notes); filler: independent loads or stores. Exceeds the 130/60 queue sizes, so queue entries are freed before retirement (c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec).

c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.text: Loads and stores complete, freeing their load/store queue entries but not their retire queue entries, once they are non-speculative
c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.quote: I'm guessing that loads and stores can complete (free their load/store queue entries, but not their retire queue entries) once they are non-speculative.
c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.notes: Tested by making the loads/stores speculative: one initial load/store whose address depends on the delay, or (in the write-up) a branch dependent on it (c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188).

c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.text: Load/store completion that frees queue entries happens in order relative to other loads and stores
c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.quote: I believe this completion is in-order relative to other loads and stores.
c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.notes: The intro states it as entries "released once they are non-speculative and all earlier loads and stores have been released".

c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.text: With a square-root delay and a branch dependent on it keeping the loads speculative, 188 loads fit before a stall
c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.quote: adding a branch, dependent on the result of the first long-latency operation ... we can run 188 loads or 118 stores without forcing the two long-latency chains to run completely in parallel
c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent B.cc (chained via FCMP, per #the-data, since FMOV might interfere); filler: loads. 188 = 130 queue + 48 scheduler + 10 dispatch queue.

c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.text: With a square-root delay and a branch dependent on it keeping the stores speculative, 118 stores fit before a stall
c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.quote: This will ensure the loads and stores cannot become non-speculative, and keep their queue entries. In this test we see we can run 188 loads or 118 stores
c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent B.cc (chained via FCMP); filler: stores. 118 = 60 store queue + 58.

c-dj-lsq-extra-58.text: The 58 entries beyond the queue sizes are the 48-entry load/store scheduler plus its 10-entry dispatch queue: integer and FP work continues while they fill, and the next load/store stalls the machine
c-dj-lsq-extra-58.quote: If the load/store scheduler and dispatch queue are full, the integer and floating point units can continue operating. But if we hit one more load/store, the machine stalls ... This explains the 58 extra entries.

c-dj-lsq-sq-60.text: Subtracting the 58 scheduler and dispatch-queue entries from the 118-store result, the store queue has 60 entries
c-dj-lsq-sq-60.quote: By this logic (subtracting 58 for the size of the scheduler and dispatch queue), the store queue has only 60 entries.
c-dj-lsq-sq-60.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent branch; filler: stores; 118 - 58. Johnson's summary: "130 load queue entries and 60 store queue entries".

c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47.text: The earlier 107-store result is 60 store-queue entries plus 47: a probe load can still enter and issue while the 48-entry scheduler has one free entry, but not once it is full
c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47.quote: So why did we think it had 47 more? Because if the 48 entry scheduler is almost full, but has one free entry, then a load can enter the scheduler, and then issue from the scheduler and execute

c-dj-lsq-x29-base.text: With cache-missing loads as the delay, the store probe gives 60 when the second delay load is based on X29 and the stores on X29 or SP, but 107 when either base register is X3 (same values)
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.quote: I tried to reproduce the "107 entry store queue" result, but the result I got was 60 entries ... Changing either or both registers back to X3 (even though the values did not change) gave me 107 again.
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.hedge: take this section with a grain of salt
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.notes: Delay: two cache-missing loads (second one X29 + variable offset); filler: stores at X29 or SP + constant offset. In a July 2022 update Johnson could not reproduce this section on an M1 Max and suspects hardware or software revisions.

c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.text: Memory dependency prediction appears to special-case X29 (the frame pointer): the load waits until it knows no older store aliases it, which it can check for up to 60 speculative stores but not 61
c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.quote: X29 is typically used as the stack frame base pointer, and I suspect the memory dependency prediction has a special case for this, and makes the load wait until it knows the store doesn't alias it.
c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.notes: Same M1 Max non-reproduction caveat as c-dj-lsq-x29-base. The intro calls it "a trick for manipulating load/store alias prediction".

c-dj-lsq-mov-counter.text: Apple's PMU has a MEMORY_ORDER_VIOLATION event, described as incorrect speculation between a store and a dependent load
c-dj-lsq-mov-counter.quote: Apple provides a performance counter for this. It's called MEMORY_ORDER_VIOLATION and described as "Incorrect speculation between store and dependent load".

c-dj-lsq-prf-not-late.text: Physical register file probes show no delay-type dependence (int+int vs int+float), so registers are neither allocated late nor freed early
c-dj-lsq-prf-not-late.quote: I do not see this kind of pattern when measuring physical register file sizes (e.g. comparing int+int vs int+float), so I believe they are neither allocated late, nor freed early.

c-dj-ice-lq-30.quote: The same logic works for Icestorm, where we see 30 load queue entries and 18 store queue entries

c-dj-ice-sq-18.quote: The same logic works for Icestorm, where we see 30 load queue entries and 18 store queue entries
c-dj-ice-sq-18.notes: The X29-based probe also measures 18 on Icestorm (#an-uncomfortable-surprising-discovery).

c-dj-ice-sched-ls-18.quote: 18 store queue entries (with an 18 entry scheduler and a 6 entry dispatch queue)

c-dj-ice-dispatch-ls-6.text: Icestorm's load/store dispatch queue has 6 entries
c-dj-ice-dispatch-ls-6.quote: with an 18 entry scheduler and a 6 entry dispatch queue

c-dj-group-issuing.text: Groups of seven uops are only observed for eliminated instructions; issuing uops are limited to roughly four per retire group
c-dj-group-issuing.quote: with issuing uops limited to roughly four per group
c-dj-group-issuing.notes: 330 groups at four issuing uops is ~1,320, not the "just over 1000" issuing window the same paragraph gives; three per group (~990) fits that window

c-dj-rename-cost.text: Every architectural register write takes a rename retire queue entry, eliminated or not: cbz and str take none, add and mov one, adds and ldp two
c-dj-rename-cost.quote: cbz or str do not require entries, add and mov need one entry, and adds or ldp need two entries

retire_groups.name: Coalesced retire groups
retire_groups.description: Uops retire in groups of up to seven; a memory op starts a group and a branch ends one.
retire_groups.detection_rule: NOP knee divided by load, store or branch knee is close to a whole number >= 2

rename_retire_queue.name: Rename retire queue (history file)
rename_retire_queue.description: A second queue of about 620 entries limits instructions that change the register map.
rename_retire_queue.detection_rule: register-writing fillers knee far below the NOP knee and above the physical register count

lsq_at_issue.name: Load/store queue entries allocated at issue
lsq_at_issue.description: Load and store queue entries are taken at issue, not at dispatch.
lsq_at_issue.detection_rule: same filler gives different knees under a miss delay and an ALU delay

register_security_tag.name: Register mapping security tag
register_security_tag.description: Reading a register the process has not written slows integer issue to about 4-wide.
register_security_tag.detection_rule: throughput drop when reading unclaimed registers

decoupled_fetch.name: Decoupled fetch with fetch-directed prefetch
decoupled_fetch.description: Fetch is not fully decoupled from branch prediction on the M1.
decoupled_fetch.detection_rule: I-cache miss cost drops under predictable branches for footprints larger than L1I

streaming_store_nt.name: Automatic non-temporal streaming stores
streaming_store_nt.description: Streaming stores become non-temporal without software hints.
streaming_store_nt.detection_rule: full-line streaming stores show no read-for-ownership traffic, so streaming write bandwidth beats partial-line writes

lsq_early_release.name: Early release of load/store queue entries
lsq_early_release.description: Loads and non-speculative stores give back their queue entries before retiring.
lsq_early_release.detection_rule: the same load or store filler gives a larger knee with no older store pending than with one

path_history_shift_xor.name: Path history register (shift-and-XOR)
path_history_shift_xor.description: The 100-bit history shifts and XORs in branch address bits, not outcomes.
path_history_shift_xor.detection_rule: two paths that differ in one bit of one earlier branch's PC or target give a spy branch with opposite outcomes ~0 % mispredicts while the bit is in the history and ~25 % (3-bit counters) once it has aged out

bpu_isolation.name: Branch predictor context isolation
bpu_isolation.description: The conditional predictor keeps no privilege or process tag.
bpu_isolation.detection_rule: out-of-place mistraining of a victim branch from another privilege level or process, with matching low-32-bit addresses and history, gives the victim ~25 % mispredicts when entries are shared and ~0 % when they are isolated

l1i_coupled_btb.name: Branch targets tied to the L1I
l1i_coupled_btb.description: A branch that misses the first-level BTB takes its target from the L1I, with a two-cycle bubble.
l1i_coupled_btb.detection_rule: taken-branch latency steps with code footprint (branch spacing) more than with branch count

zero_cycle_loads.name: Zero-cycle loads (register-file memory renaming)
zero_cycle_loads.description: A load from a just-stored address is renamed to the register holding the stored value.
zero_cycle_loads.detection_rule: a store and reload through the same base register shortens a load-to-DIV dependency chain; the same address through a different register does not

banked_prf_power.name: Banked register file with bank power gating
banked_prf_power.description: The register file has four banks that power down separately; waking one costs two or three cycles.
banked_prf_power.detection_rule: a small extra delay at the register-exhaustion knee that appears or vanishes when the delay changes by one cycle

dispatch_buffers.name: Two-level dispatch through unordered buffers
dispatch_buffers.description: Rename writes into unordered dispatch buffers that feed one scheduler queue per unit.
dispatch_buffers.detection_rule: after a long run of ADDs, rename-only instructions (MOV, NOP) run free for about buffer size / drain rate cycles; a filler limited to three integer units fills a 12-entry buffer, not 24

paired_sched_queues.name: Paired scheduler queues
paired_sched_queues.description: Scheduler queues are paired; a queue with nothing ready issues from its partner.
paired_sched_queues.detection_rule: a filler that can issue to only one unit of a pair sees about half the queue capacity of one that can issue to both

immediate_regs.name: Immediate register pool written at rename
immediate_regs.description: A MOV of a non-zero immediate completes at rename into a pool of about 36 registers.
immediate_regs.detection_rule: a MOV #imm filler knee lies about 36-38 above the ADD knee, and up to ~36 padded MOV #imm placed before ADDs do not move the ADD knee

l2_cachelets.name: Per-core L2 cachelets (inner and outer L2)
l2_cachelets.description: The 12 MiB L2 behaves as four 3 MiB cachelets, one beside each core.
l2_cachelets.detection_rule: single-core bandwidth sweeps step at ~3 MiB and ~7.5 MiB, short of the 12 MiB L2

dczva_l2_zero.name: DC ZVA zero-allocates lines in L2
dczva_l2_zero.description: DC ZVA allocates zeroed lines directly in the L2.
dczva_l2_zero.detection_rule: a DC ZVA stream beats the plain-store fill rate beyond L1 and shows no L1 writebacks

nt_load_handling.name: Non-temporal loads skip L1 fill
nt_load_handling.description: Non-temporal loads are not prefetched into the L1.
nt_load_handling.detection_rule: LDNPQ vs LDPQ sweep is equal in L1, LDNPQ lower in L2 with a higher L1 miss count, higher in DRAM

dtlb_piggyback.name: Single-ported dTLB with piggyback ports
dtlb_piggyback.description: One dTLB lookup per cycle, shared with queued requests to the same page.
dtlb_piggyback.detection_rule: three loads per cycle to one page run at full rate; spreading them over three pages 16 KiB apart drops to about 2.5 cycles per three loads, and a new page on every access to about one load per cycle

l1d_banked_piggyback.name: Banked L1D with piggybacked loads and buffered stores
l1d_banked_piggyback.description: Sixteen 16 B banks; loads to one element share an access and stores are buffered.
l1d_banked_piggyback.detection_rule: loads stepping by 256 B fall to one per cycle, by 128 B to about 1.7 and by 64 B to about 2.35, while steps up to 32 B keep three per cycle; stores keep two per cycle out to 128 B steps

l1d_way_lookup.name: L1D way selection without visible misprediction
l1d_way_lookup.description: Loads to random ways run as fast as loads to one way; no way misprediction shows.
l1d_way_lookup.detection_rule: loads that pick one of eight 16 KiB-apart pages at random on every access run no slower than loads to a fixed page once bank collisions are removed

lsu_virtual_prefetch.name: LSU-resident virtual-address prefetcher
lsu_virtual_prefetch.description: The prefetcher trains on every load and store virtual address at the LSU.
lsu_virtual_prefetch.detection_rule: a linear pointer chase keeps its L1 latency across page boundaries out to DRAM, and page-strided chains the prefetcher can follow lose the L1 TLB miss cost; a physical-address prefetcher would restart at each page

l1d_hashed_way.name: L1D way chosen from physical page bits
l1d_hashed_way.description: A line's way seems fixed by a hash of physical page bits.
l1d_hashed_way.detection_rule: pointer chases with node spacing 2^k+64 B reach the full L1 line count for some k and about one way per set for others, with no extra-cycle way-mispredict outliers

content_directed_prefetch.name: Content-directed (data memory-dependent) prefetch
content_directed_prefetch.description: Pointer-like values in filled lines are prefetched into the L2.
content_directed_prefetch.detection_rule: loading a line of pointers makes later chases through those pointers faster although no load ever used their addresses

scan_on_fill_nfp.name: Scan-on-fill next-fetch predictor
scan_on_fill_nfp.description: Prefetched instruction lines are scanned for branches before their first use.
scan_on_fill_nfp.detection_rule: after a predictor flush, later taken branches in a recently filled line redirect faster than the first

loop_modes.name: Tiered loop modes
loop_modes.description: Loops run from the instruction queue, a loop buffer or an L0 cache.
loop_modes.detection_rule: a loop body shorter than the 8-wide dispatch group sustaining more than one iteration (taken loop-back branch) per cycle would show loop packing
